extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and computer scientists writing papers, books, exercises, proofs, algorithms, and literate programs (students and authors preparing technical exposition)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for clear, correct, and readable mathematical and computer-science writing, typesetting, and literate programming—covering notation, formulas, sentence/paragraph style, proofreading, book production, and module design. Intended to help authors prepare papers, textbooks, algorithms, exercises, and WEB/Pascal-style programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation formatting for vectors
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a consistent and context-appropriate style for vectors (e.g., boldface symbols or arrows over vectors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either boldface or arrow notation is appropriate depending on context; pick a convention and use it consistently throughout the document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superscript textual endings (e.g., 'st') in roman type
rubrics_metrics.description: When using a raised 'st' in phrases such as '1st' (or similar textual superscripts), use roman type rather than math italics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use roman type for textual superscripts so that it's clear you aren't speaking of a mathematical component; keep textual and mathematical typography distinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'psychologically bad' line breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't let the final symbol of a sentence lie on a line separate from the rest of its sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use non-breaking spaces (e.g., a tilde in TeX) or processor-specific methods to tie symbols/words together to avoid awkward breaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use spelling checkers
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors who are not strong spellers should learn to use spelling-checking tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on spelling checkers to catch many mistakes; proofreading is still necessary for technical correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep formulas reasonably short ('name and conquer')
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid allowing formulas to get so long that they don't format well or become unnecessarily confusing; prefer giving subexpressions names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce names or new symbols to keep expressions tractable; long formulae that force awkward manipulation should be reorganized or renamed for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be stingy with quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid overusing quotation marks; excessive quoted phrases look cute and can distract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quotes only when necessary (e.g., quoting an exact phrase); avoid putting many short quoted items in a row.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize subscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid excessive or deeply nested subscripts which can be hard to read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose notation that reduces subscript clutter; consider renaming or reorganizing indices when subscripts become confusing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize theorem/lemma/fact names in titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Words like 'Theorem' and 'Lemma' should be capitalized in titles (e.g., 'Lemma 1', 'Theorem 23').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow conventional capitalization in headings and labels to aid readability and consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place words between adjacent formulas to avoid ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: Insert words between adjacent inline formulas to prevent grammatically ambiguous phrases (e.g., 'Add k times to c' is ambiguous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restructure sentences so mathematical items are clearly connected to surrounding prose; adding short words often disambiguates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define symbols before (or very near) use
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful to define symbols before you use them, or at least very close to their first occurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce notation clearly at first mention; avoid long spans between introduction and use of a symbol.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid monotonous sentence openings
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't get hung up on one or two styles of sentence openers (e.g., 'Thus,', 'Consequently,', 'Therefore,') which can become very monotonous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary sentence structure unless parallelism is intentionally used for rhetorical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use parallelism when it serves a point
rubrics_metrics.description: Parallel structure should be used when it supports the point you're making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply parallel phrasing deliberately (e.g., in lists or paired constructions) to emphasize relationships; otherwise vary phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make sentences comprehensible left-to-right
rubrics_metrics.description: Write sentences so readers can parse them as they read from left to right; avoid structures that momentarily mislead about what's being proved or asserted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rephrase sentences like 'We prove that (A) and (B) implies (C)' to 'We prove that the two conditions (A) and (B) imply (C)' to avoid temporary misreading that (A) and (B) are being proved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place the word 'that' by cadence and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on using or omitting 'that' should be driven by cadence and clarity; read sentences aloud to decide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If inclusion or omission of 'that' improves clarity and rhythm, follow that choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'shall' with audience awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: The word 'shall' is traditional in definitions but may sound formal to younger readers; consider audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer less formal wording for a modern or younger audience; for formal legal/standard definitions 'shall' may still be appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be precise in logical wording
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose words that precisely express logical meaning (e.g., 'not nonincreasing' is not the same as 'increasing').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure wording matches the mathematical property intended; avoid colloquial substitutions that change logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid passive voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer active constructions (e.g., replace 'It can be shown...' with 'A proof shows...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use active voice to make exposition direct and clear; passive voice can hide the agent and make arguments less engaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixed tenses on the same subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not switch tenses awkwardly within the same subject or sentence (avoid mixing present with future constructions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep tense consistent unless there's a clear temporal reason to change it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer explicit phrasing for proofs by contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the ungainly phrase 'Assume by contradiction that (blah)'; instead say 'The proof that (blah) is by contradiction' or 'To prove (X), let us assume the opposite and see what happens.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear, reader-friendly phrasing for proof structures; explain method before launching into steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a conversational tone with signposts
rubrics_metrics.description: A conversational tone with signposts and clear transition paragraphs improves readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrases like 'We divide the proof into two parts...' or 'The operative word is...' act as helpful signposts; use them to guide the reader through long arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be consistent and clear in relation notation and ordering
rubrics_metrics.description: When giving relations, choose a form that is easy to visualize (e.g., 'Pi < Pj' vs 'Pi Pj') and keep ordering consistent (e.g., index ordering positions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer forms that match readers' expectations and be consistent about index order and relative positions to avoid confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewriting and multiple drafts are essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Good writing demands many passes: compose (hand or terminal), then edit for flow while typing, then typeset and revise multiple times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors often find different issues at different passes; don't expect the first draft to be final—rewriting is valuable, but at some point you must publish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use professional book designers and copy editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Author self-publishing should still value the services of professional designers and copy editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers control page plans, fonts, heading styles, margins; copy editors catch punctuation, style, and consistency issues—hire them when feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish mathematical numerals from text numerals in typefaces
rubrics_metrics.description: When using typefaces like Euler, distinguish mathematical zeros and numerals from text numerals (the glyphs may differ intentionally).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful manuscript preparation is required so that the math glyphs and text glyphs are correctly used and recognizable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read at speed to check rhythm and flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading prose at normal speed reveals rhythm issues and helps detect sentences that need smoothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice reading text aloud or at speed to find stilted or awkward constructions to be revised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid displaying false equations as real
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not display false equations in the text without clearly indicating their falsity—readers may treat displayed equations as authoritative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need to show a false equation as an example, put it inline with a clarifying phrase like 'the equation ... is always false!'

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure clear antecedents for pronouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure any pronoun's antecedent is clear; avoid sentences like multiple 'It is...' constructions that could be ambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace vague 'it' with explicit nouns when necessary; rewrite sentences with ambiguous pronoun references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid page breaks in the middle of displayed formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not allow page breaks to split displayed formulas; adjust surrounding text or add material to keep the formula on one page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think of filling the page or rephrasing text to move the display intact to the next page; treat this as a necessary final-stage edit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let proofs follow the same order as definitions when handling cases
rubrics_metrics.description: When a proof must deal with several cases, present the proof in the same order the definitions or cases were introduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keeping the same order helps readers follow case distinctions and matches natural exposition order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish hyphen, en-dash, minus sign, and em-dash
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphens, en-dashes, minus signs, and em-dashes are distinct typographic symbols and should not be used interchangeably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the shortest (hyphen) for compounds, en-dash for ranges (e.g., 'lines 10–18'), minus sign for mathematical subtraction, and em-dash for sentence breaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofread for mathematical correctness as well as style
rubrics_metrics.description: When proofreading, check both typographical/stylistic errors and the mathematics itself (e.g., ambiguous limits or incorrect statements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correct mathematical language (e.g., 'x decreases to 0' vs 'x → 0 through negative values') where necessary; consult domain knowledge during edits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about contrast words like 'instead'
rubrics_metrics.description: When using 'instead', clarify the contrast explicitly so the reader immediately understands what is being referred to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace vague contrasts like 'And when x = -1 instead' with 'And when x = -1 instead of +1...' to make the contrast explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use present tense for timeless facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use present tense for facts that remain true; past tense may be used for results that were later shown false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., known theorems remain stated in present tense; historical narrative may use past tense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary repetition of words
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't repeat words in close proximity when synonyms or rephrasing can improve clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tools like thesauruses and careful editing to vary language and avoid clumsy repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use page numbers sparingly for local references
rubrics_metrics.description: Give page numbers only for remote references; for nearby items use direct references like 'Equation 5.14'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Number tables by the page on which they appear (the 'freeway method') may be convenient in some contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose formula variants for clarity (reorder factors/signs)
rubrics_metrics.description: You may rewrite a formula (e.g., change sign placement or reorder factors) if an alternative form is clearer for readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propagate the change consistently through subsequent text and references (e.g., change 'k - r/2' to 'r/2 - k' everywhere if needed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be consistent about placement of integral limits and similar notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to place integral limits above/below the sign or to the right, and be consistent throughout a book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both forms are used; trade-offs include vertical vs horizontal space. Pick one for the entire work unless justified exceptions exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: When long formulas don't fit, break lines logically or change math
rubrics_metrics.description: If a long formula won't fit well, either break it at logical points or introduce new symbols to simplify presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should decide how to display complex expressions; moving from inline to displayed form or changing notation to allow natural breaks is acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line-break rule around equals sign for embedded vs displayed formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: For line breaks in the middle of embedded formulas the break comes after the equals sign; in a display the break comes before the equals sign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the conventional placement to preserve readability and expected alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust punctuation and paragraph breaks to control flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Change semicolons to periods or vice versa and break long paragraphs into smaller ones to adjust the rhythm and clarity of exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sentence and paragraph boundaries deliberately to affect reading speed and comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose clear and non-misleading variable names
rubrics_metrics.description: Variable names should not be misleading or too similar to conceptually unrelated variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic renaming (aided by text editors) can reduce confusion; pick names that reflect role or type clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overuse of stacked fractions; prefer slashed forms when practical
rubrics_metrics.description: Stacked fractions with horizontal bars can produce tiny numbers or awkward spacing; slashed forms (a/b) often read better in running text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copy editors often replace stacked fractions with slashed forms and add parentheses as needed; consider slashed forms especially in exponents or small type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercises require extra clarity and redundancy
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercises have little context and are hard to translate; ambiguity is especially harmful, so include carefully chosen redundancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about assumptions, notation, and desired deliverables in exercises; credit previous sources for exercises as required by copyright rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answers to exercises can be short and start with a symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: In exercise answer sections, concise and pithy answers (even starting with a symbol) are acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relax some rhetorical rules for exercise answers to allow efficient communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write algorithms in accessible notation (often English) rather than a specific language
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid alienating readers, present algorithms in English with numbered steps and high-level comments rather than commit to a single programming language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don's approach: present algorithms like theorems with labeled steps and parenthetical comments; if a programming language is used, be mindful of readership and conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fixed-width fonts for displayed computer programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Displayed programs should use fixed-width type and consistent fonts so that code is readable and symbols aren't confused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers may need to mix styles (roman, bold, italic) with fixed-width; insist on fixed-width where appropriate for program listings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literate programming: break complex things into parts and explain twice
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain complex material by breaking it into parts and presenting each part informally and formally (i.e., explain twice: informal text and formal code).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WEB systems allow a single source file to produce typeset documentation or program source; author modules to first motivate and then formalize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce modules at the psychologically right moment
rubrics_metrics.description: In literate programming, each module should be introduced when it makes sense for reader motivation rather than strict top-to-bottom order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ordering helps readers learn ideas in the sequence the author discovered them and preserves natural exposition order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Module contents: provide informal but clear descriptions, not play-by-play
rubrics_metrics.description: Each module should include an informal high-level description of what it does (not a low-level step-through).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convey intuition and purpose rather than a line-by-line account; aim to help the reader understand the role of the module.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep modules small and manageable (≈ a dozen lines)
rubrics_metrics.description: Don suggests modules of about a dozen lines of code; very long modules should be split into smaller pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break large modules into tractable parts to reflect the philosophy of decomposing a complex system into manageable components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use imperative names for action modules, descriptors for declarative modules
rubrics_metrics.description: Name modules with imperatives for actions (e.g., 'Store the word in the dictionary') and descriptors for declarative lists (e.g., 'Procedures for sorting').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalizing the first letter of a module name is natural; choose naming conventions that clarify the module's role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid carrying obsolete conventions into new styles
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't keep old-style conventions (e.g., 'end { while }' comments used in Pascal) that are unnecessary or redundant in newer styles like WEB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adopting a new system, shed irrelevant baggage and follow the conventions appropriate to the new style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifier naming: avoid awkward camelCase with uppercase after lowercase
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifiers like 'FindinNewWord3' look bad in print; prefer joining words with short underscores (e.g., 'get_word') or other readable conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use naming approaches that render well in print and are readable; WEB/TANGLE can remove underscores when producing code for compilers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anthropomorphize system prompts consistently when helpful
rubrics_metrics.description: Using 'I' for a computer prompt can make interfaces easier to conceptualize; consistency in whether you use 'we' or 'it' to describe program actions matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide on an anthropomorphic stance (e.g., 'we insert the element' vs 'it inserts the element') and keep it consistent throughout documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't start sentences with symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid starting sentences with a mathematical symbol; sentences beginning with symbols are awkward and easily rewritten.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrite to begin with words or embed the symbol within a grammatical structure (e.g., 'Assume the data...' instead of 'data assumes...').

rubrics_metrics.name: Write user manuals for the absolute novice
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim manuals at absolute novices: avoid jargon that even some experts may be uncomfortable with while ensuring novices can follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you succeed in writing for novices, experts will still understand; otherwise you risk communicating with nobody. Watch for hidden jargon that authors acquire over time.
